extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of rhetoric/oratory; teachers of rhetoric; classical readers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how to develop effective eloquence: theoretical rules are necessary but must be joined to a firm facility (habit/skill) developed through writing, reading, and speaking. Considers whether any single practice mode can suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of rhetorical precepts
rubrics_metrics.description: sed haec eloquendi praecepta, sicut cogitationi sunt necessaria, ita non satis ad vim dicendi valent
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quintilian states that the precepts or rules of eloquence are necessary to thought (they structure thinking) but by themselves do not suffice to produce the force or power of speaking; theoretical knowledge alone is inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of a firm facility (hexis)
rubrics_metrics.description: nisi illis firma quaedam facilitas, quae apud Graecos ἕξις nominatur, accesserit
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective speaking requires a 'firm facility' or habitual ease (Greek ἕξις) in addition to rules — i.e., practiced skill, readiness, and fluency that must be acquired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice modes: writing, reading, speaking
rubrics_metrics.description: ad quam scribendo plus an legendo an dicendo conferatur, solere quaeri scio
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quintilian notes the common question of which activity contributes most to developing facility — writing, reading, or speaking — implying that these are the principal modes of training to consider and compare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine whether a single mode suffices
rubrics_metrics.description: quod esset diligentius nobis examinandum, si qualibet earum rerum possemus una esse contenti
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One should carefully examine whether one of these activities alone could be sufficient; the passage implies skepticism about relying on a single method and recommends deliberate evaluation of a balanced regimen.
